visualVerification.source: H:/Ancient Japan History/ch2/ch2.pdf (55 pages, printed pp. 108-162) checked against H:/Ancient Japan History/ch2/ch2 - raw OCR.txt
visualVerification.method: Full 55-page contact-sheet review; direct full-page inspection of the opening, final page, and map plates on printed pp. 115, 148, and 150; searchable PDF text checked page by page against the primary OCR for headings, names, chronology, inscriptions, quotations, and map captions.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 108-110; OCR opening and three currents of Yamato change
substanceRetained: Yamato's later-third- through sixth-century development, the meaning of kofun, and the source's vigor-expansion-disruption architecture.
The evidentiary problem created by the absence of contemporary Japanese narrative records and the need to combine archaeology, foreign histories, and later chronicles.
omittedAs: Long bibliographic survey of postwar scholars
Obsolete horse-rider conquest certainty
supplementalSources: ch02-research-notes.md: current terminology, evidence boundaries, and Kofun interpretation.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 110-112; OCR northeast Asia, Lelang, the Korean kingdoms, continental migration, and the Gwanggaeto inscription
substanceRetained: The post-Han political setting, destruction of Lelang, formation of Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla, and the importance of peninsular routes.
The 414 stele as evidence for Wa participation in peninsular war, with its rhetoric and damaged text treated cautiously.
omittedAs: Footnote-level historiography
Any implication that cultural transfer was a one-way civilizing process
supplementalSources: ch02-research-notes.md: Gaya as multiple autonomous polities and long reciprocal migration.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 112-115; OCR Ancient mounds, Yayoi precedents, Tatetsuki, Makimuku, haniwa, and Map 2.1
substanceRetained: Late Yayoi mound traditions as predecessors rather than a sudden Yamato invention.
The rise of the Shiki royal cluster, its scale, succession pattern, grave goods, and capacity to mobilize labor.
omittedAs: Catalog-style repetition of every measurement where the argument does not change
OCR corruption inside Map 2.1
supplementalSources: The scalable Map 2A reproduces the chapter's internal geography with a documented legend.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 115-117; OCR Makimuku irrigation, agricultural growth, Mount Miwa, and Omiwa ritual
substanceRetained: The connection between iron tools, irrigation, agricultural surplus, and royal monument building.
Mount Miwa as sacred body and the material geography joining early kingship to an established cult.
omittedAs: Unqualified causal claims that one agricultural innovation alone created Yamato

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 117-119; OCR Sujin revelations, Otataneko, Momoso-hime, Hashihaka, military traditions, and the Saki shift
substanceRetained: The chronicle traditions connecting kingship, calamity, correct Miwa worship, sacred marriage, and Hashihaka.
The coexistence of sacral and military functions, with myths separated from contemporary event evidence.
omittedAs: Early Mimana tribute treated as historical fact
Literal biographical identification of Hashihaka's occupant

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 119-121; OCR Saki mounds, Yamato Takeru traditions, Isonokami, Inishiki, Mononobe, and sacred weapons
substanceRetained: The shift to Saki as a change in political geography and the heroic traditions as memories of expansion rather than campaign logs.
Isonokami's storehouses, weapon cult, and retrospective linkage of military custody to the Mononobe.
omittedAs: Chronicle reign-year precision for mythic episodes

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 121-124; OCR Seven-Branched Sword, Paekche diplomacy, fourth-century wars, status debate, and peninsular contact
substanceRetained: The sword's form, inscription, common 369 reading, diplomatic presentation, iron context, and later Isonokami custody.
Baekje-Goguryeo-Silla relations and the limits of using gift language to prove a fixed interstate hierarchy.
omittedAs: Nationalist superior-versus-inferior polemic
Mimana or Gaya described as a settled Yamato colony
supplementalSources: ch02-research-notes.md: modern Gaya and cross-strait exchange framework.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed p. 124; OCR Okinoshima, Munakata, maritime offerings, and synthesis of early Yamato vigor
substanceRetained: Okinoshima's fourth- through ninth-century ritual sequence, maritime safety, peninsular objects, and Munakata's strategic alliance with the court.
omittedAs: Excavation bibliography
supplementalSources: UNESCO Okinoshima documentation summarized in ch02-research-notes.md.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 125-129; OCR Yamato Expansion, Kawachi-Izumi, Mozu-Furuichi tombs, grave goods, Ojin-Nintoku traditions, and royal-line debate
substanceRetained: The post-400 shift, alternating tomb clusters, monumental scale, level-ground construction, military assemblages, and a more maritime kingship.
The iri-wake naming argument, Yasojima ritual, and Jingu-Ojin traditions retained as evidence for remembered discontinuity, not an invasion proof.
omittedAs: Exact labor estimate presented as a verified count
Unqualified attribution of imperial-designated tombs to named rulers
supplementalSources: UNESCO Mozu-Furuichi documentation summarized in ch02-research-notes.md.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 129-131; OCR Ishikawa and Mamuta waterworks, immigrant technicians, Naniwa, Sumiyoshi, and maritime power
substanceRetained: The productive and political importance of canals, dikes, Korean immigrant knowledge, and the Mamuta gourd-sacrifice story.
Naniwa as harbor hinge and Sumiyoshi as the sacred articulation of overseas movement.
omittedAs: A celebratory account of public works that erases coercive and dependent labor

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 131-133; OCR outlying regions, Upper Kenu tombs, court-linked coffins, Inariyama and Eta Funayama swords
substanceRetained: Regional tomb sequences as evidence for incorporation through local leaders rather than uniform direct administration.
Contemporary sword inscriptions linking distant elites, military groups, genealogies, and the title great king.
omittedAs: The claim that a shared tomb style automatically proves complete court control

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 133-140; OCR mechanisms of control, farming communities, uji, kabane, Ingyo ordeal, tomo, be, immigrants, and craft groups
substanceRetained: The agrarian and sacred bases of corporate lineages, the ranking functions of kabane, and inscriptional evidence for the system.
Occupational groups as producers of military, ritual, agricultural, craft, and administrative capacity, including the central role of immigrants.
omittedAs: Long later register examples where one clear example carries the argument
Language that treats dependent immigrant labor as a frictionless gift

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 140-144; OCR foreign expansion, hostages, Southern Song missions, Five Kings of Wa, 475 crisis, Yuryaku memorial, and material motives
substanceRetained: The changing Baekje-Wa and Goguryeo-Silla alignments, hostage diplomacy, and ten Southern Song missions between 421 and 478.
The 478 memorial's claims and limitations, Baekje's 475 defeat, Chinese titles, and the movement of iron, prestige goods, and specialists.
omittedAs: Long quotation from the copyrighted translation paraphrased instead
Royal claims of scores of conquered kingdoms treated as fact

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 145-151; OCR Keitai, peninsular reverses, new Nara base, changing tombs, Iwai rebellion, Kyushu zones, Iwatoyama, and Map 2.3
substanceRetained: Contested continuity at Keitai's accession, concessions to Baekje, failed mobilization, the progressive loss of Gaya influence, and the southwestern Nara shift.
Iwai's regional strength, Tsukushi's strategic geography, and archaeological confirmation at Iwatoyama.
omittedAs: Buretsu's moralized cruelty accepted as biography
The geographically obsolete idea of one Mimana kingdom absorbed in 531
OCR-corrupted Map 2.3 labels
supplementalSources: ch02-research-notes.md: Gaya remained a confederated field whose final major polity fell in 562.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 152-159; OCR royal estates, Kasuya, Nanotsu, Musashi, Kibi, policy disputes, registration, scribes, districts, and foreign affairs
substanceRetained: The shift from central household estates to strategic regional miyake after conflict and the examples of Kyushu, Musashi, and Kibi.
Household registration, scribal titles, agata supervisors, the 540 policy turn, and the growing value of literate management.
omittedAs: Every estate in the chronicle's compressed 535 list
Anachronistic equation of these offices with the finished ritsuryo system
supplementalSources: The scalable Map 2A includes Kibi, Kyushu, Kanto, the Nara core, and route context.

coverage.sourceRange: PDF printed pp. 159-162; OCR mid-sixth-century knowledge transfers, Buddhism, Soga origins, Iname, Umako, succession wars, Sushun, and Suiko
substanceRetained: The exchange of troops and continental learning, disputed formal Buddhist introduction, and the move toward text-centered government.
Soga wealth, immigrant and estate connections, in-law marriage strategy, Mononobe defeat, Sushun's assassination, and Suiko's 593 enthronement.
omittedAs: The source's erroneous placement of Yomei's accession in 587
Later anti-Soga moral judgment treated as neutral fact
supplementalSources: ch02-research-notes.md: date and terminology corrections; Chapter 3 will develop Buddhism in full.
